conversation.content:
Hello! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my sole job today is to listen and understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days; it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can crop up after childbirth, and it includes a check-in about any thoughts of self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might hurt yourself or someone else. If that happens, we’ll work together to get you immediate help. There are no right or wrong answers, and you can pause any time. When you’re ready, we’ll begin. Let’s start with question one:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things, or has enjoyment felt hard to come by?

[soft exhale]  
Most things feel… flat. I can still get a little spark when my sister sends me cute videos or when the baby actually smiles, but it’s nowhere near the lift I used to feel. It’s like the color’s been drained out of stuff I normally like—half the time I think “I should be excited” but it just doesn’t land.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, eyes on hands]  
Not really… I’ll see something that’s supposed to be funny—like a silly meme my partner shows me—and I can feel a tiny smile, but it’s gone in a second. Most days I don’t laugh at all. I just feel too tired or heavy inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet pause]  
Hardly. I wake up thinking “what’s the point?” I still try—like, I tell myself I should want that coffee meet-up my friend planned—but when it actually comes close, the excitement just isn’t there. It feels like I’m going through motions for everyone else, not because I truly look forward to anything anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the floor]  
Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” The other night he wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking it must be my milk, or that I’m just not soothing him right. Even spilled milk on the counter—illogical as it sounds—I caught myself muttering “of course I can’t even pour properly.” I know it’s not all my fault, but those guilty thoughts pop up several times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. My heart races the moment I put him in the crib—what if he spits up and chokes? I’ll check the monitor every few minutes even when he’s quiet. There’s no real danger, but the thoughts just loop, and I can’t settle unless I peek in on him again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands a little]  
A few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight and it feels like I can’t get enough air—like last night when I was folding laundry. No reason for it, but for a couple of minutes I thought something awful was about to happen. It passes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, my phone buzzes, and suddenly it feels like too much. I’ll stand in the kitchen just staring because I don’t know which thing to do first, and my chest gets heavy. I get it done eventually, but it feels way harder than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
That’s been most nights. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—going over everything I might have done wrong, worrying the baby will wake up any second. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and even then I jerk awake once or twice with my heart racing. By morning I’m just as tired as when I went to bed.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes well up a little]  
Yeah… pretty much every day. There’s this heavy sadness that sits on me from the moment I open my eyes. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I just feel empty or like I want to cry. It lifts for a few minutes here and there, but it always settles back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, voice cracks]  
Yes… maybe twice this week. Yesterday I put him in the car seat and couldn’t get the buckle right on the first try—such a dumb thing—and I just burst into tears. I sat on the floor crying for maybe ten minutes, feeling like I’m failing at even the simplest stuff.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, eyes fixed on the floor]  
Once or twice… just fleeting. Like I’ll be standing at the top of the stairs and think, “What if I just fell?” It’s gone as fast as it comes, and I’d never do anything—I couldn’t leave my baby—but the idea has popped in, maybe twice in the past week. I haven’t told anyone that.

You've shared how the joy and colour seem to have drained from life since your baby arrived: laughter feels distant, excitement is replaced by a flat "what's the point?", and ordinary tasks feel overwhelming. Each day brings heavy sadness, nightly worry-ridden insomnia, sudden panicky moments, and repeated self-blame over tiny parenting hurdles. You mentioned fleeting thoughts of falling down the stairs, quickly dismissed but frightening to you. Your openness highlights how hard you're trying while feeling you're "failing at even the simplest stuff."
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports virtually no laughter and only fleeting amusement, aligning with "Not at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "Hardly" and describes complete absence of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming thoughts "several times a day" and gives multiple examples, indicating this happens most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, looping worries without real danger, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic episodes with chest tightness and breathlessness occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to prioritize tasks, and experiencing physical anxiety, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disturbance linked to unhappiness, intrusive thoughts, and anxiety—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, pervasive sadness and emptiness, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying twice this week, triggered by minor frustration, matching "Yes, quite often" (2).</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 26 well exceeds the 14-point high-risk cutoff, with item scores of 3 on 8 of 10 items, indicating severe symptom frequency. Her narrative aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: daily depressed mood and markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) for more than two weeks plus guilt, hopelessness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and recurrent passive suicidal ideation without intent. Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, constant worry about the baby) suggest probable <med>generalized anxiety disorder</med> or <med>panic attacks</med> in addition to depression. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist to discuss safety, medication options compatible with breastfeeding, and therapy referrals
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Begin weekly evidence-based therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) specializing in postpartum mood disorders
4. Plan daily 20-minute mood-boosting activity (short walk outdoors, guided meditation, gentle postpartum exercise) and enlist partner or friend to ensure time is protected
5. Practice sleep-hygiene: split night duties with support person, limit screen time after feeds, use relaxation breathing when mind races
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS and clinical review within 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
(10-item Edinburgh-based interview, gestational week 6–8)

A. Self-reported symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (daily)  
- Marked guilt/self-blame over routine infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, panic spells without clear trigger  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to ruminative worry  
- Feeling overwhelmed by minor tasks, “drowning” most days  
- Passive, fleeting self-harm ideation (twice this week; denied intent/plan)

B. Pattern  
All responses cluster in the severe range; symptoms present “pretty much every day” and interfere with basic functioning.

C. Screening significance / risk flags  
1. Meets cutoff indicators for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset.  
2. Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (GAD & panic) requiring additional assessment.  
3. Passive suicidal ideation present → elevated safety risk necessitating immediate clinical evaluation.

D. Summary  
Client endorses pervasive depressive and anxious symptoms exceeding two-week duration, with functional impairment and first-time disclosure of passive self-harm thoughts. Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist and same-day safety planning.
